cards.text: This psalm opens with the writer talking to his own soul, then turning to speak to the LORD. He tells the LORD He is very great, clothed with splendor and majesty. And friend, he's just getting warmed up.

cards.question: The writer pictures the LORD dressed in splendor. What does the LORD wrap Himself in like a garment?

cards.text: He wears LIGHT, friend. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer begging for one little slice of light, and He puts it on like a jacket.
He stretches out the heavens like a tent and lays the beams of His chambers in the waters above. Then the writer pictures Him on the move.

cards.question: The writer pictures the LORD riding across the sky. What does He make His chariot?
The writer says the LORD treats the winds and the flames of fire as His enemies.

cards.text: Now the writer looks down at the earth, set on its foundations, never to be moved. That's steadier than anything I've ever stood on, and friend, I stand on GOLD.

cards.question: In the next picture, the mountains are hidden. What covered the earth like a garment, standing above the mountains?
Then the LORD rebukes the waters covering the earth. What do they do?

cards.text: At the sound of His thunder, they hurry away. Like a break room clearing out the second the boss pokes his head in asking who's free Saturday.
The mountains rise and the valleys sink, each one to the place God assigned for it.

cards.question: Then God sets a boundary the waters cannot cross. Why?

answers.text: So they never cover the earth again
So the ships can sail safely
So the fish stay in one place

cards.text: Next, God sends springs into the valleys, flowing between the mountains.

cards.question: Who does the writer say the springs in the valleys give drink to?

cards.text: The birds nest beside the springs and sing among the branches. God waters the mountains from His chambers, and the earth is satisfied by the fruit of His works.

cards.question: God makes the grass grow for the ___ and provides crops for people to cultivate.

cards.text: From the earth comes wine that gladdens the heart, oil that makes a face shine, and bread that sustains the heart. Not just enough to get by, friend. Gladness too.

cards.question: The trees of the LORD have their fill, including the cedars of Lebanon. Who planted those cedars?

cards.text: Birds nest in those trees, the stork makes her home in the cypresses, the wild goats get the high mountains, and the rock badgers find refuge in the cliffs. Ducking into the cliffs? That's me behind the cooling racks every time a batch comes out burnt.

cards.question: Trees, birds, storks, goats and rock badgers. What's the big picture the writer paints here?

answers.text: God gives each creature its place
Every creature must fight for space
People rule over the wild places

cards.text: Now the writer looks up: God made the moon to mark the seasons, and the sun knows when to set. The SUN knows when to clock out, friend, and I've got a timer AND I still burn a batch.

cards.question: When God brings darkness and it becomes night, the beasts of the forest settle down to sleep.

cards.text: Night is when the beasts of the forest prowl. The young lions roar for their prey.

cards.question: Those roaring young lions are hungry. Who does the writer say they seek their food from?
When the sun rises, the young lions withdraw and lie down in their ___.

cards.text: The lions clock out, and people clock in. Man goes out to his work and his labor until evening.
Then the writer says, "How many are Your works, O LORD!" Friend, I lose count of my cookie boxes before lunch.

cards.question: The writer says the earth is full of God's creatures. What did God make them all in?

cards.text: Then he points to the sea, vast and wide, teeming with creatures great and small. Ships pass there, and so does Leviathan.

cards.question: Out in that vast sea is Leviathan. What does the writer say God formed Leviathan to do there?
All of God's creatures look to Him to give them something in due season. What is it?

cards.text: When God gives it, they gather it up, and when He opens His hand, they're satisfied with good things. Like a whole office the second somebody cracks open a cookie box in the break room.

cards.question: When God hides His face, the creatures are terrified. When He takes away their breath, what happens?

answers.text: They die and return to dust
They fall into a deep sleep
They wander off to the sea

cards.question: When God sends His Spirit, creatures are ___ and He renews the face of the earth.

cards.text: Then the writer says, "May the glory of the LORD endure forever; may the LORD rejoice in His works." And when the LORD looks on the earth, it trembles.

cards.question: The earth trembles when the LORD looks at it. What happens when He touches the mountains?
After looking at everything God made, how long does the writer say he will sing to the LORD?

cards.text: Then the writer says, "May my meditation be pleasing to Him, for I rejoice in the LORD." And he adds, "May sinners vanish from the earth and the wicked be no more."

cards.question: The psalm ends with the same line it started with, followed by a Hallelujah. What is that line?

answers.text: Bless the LORD O my soul

findings.problem: This story card only restates the answer to card 2 (He wears light) and adds a joke. It tells no new part of the passage, so it is a recap card. Card 4 then goes back to tell the rest of verse 2. The joke should ride on a card that moves the passage forward, such as card 4.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.

findings.problem: Verse 4 is covered only by a false true-or-false statement (the winds and flames are His enemies). No card ever tells the baker what the verse actually says: He makes the winds His messengers and flames of fire His servants. The baker leaves without that detail. Unlike stop 2 card 2, no story card follows to tell the real picture.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: This story card has 3 sentences: the wine, oil and bread sentence, then "Not just enough to get by, friend." and then "Gladness too." It is not the opening card.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The question asks who the lions seek their food from. The answers are not the same kind of thing: "From God" is a person, "From the farmers' flocks" is animals and "From the riverbanks" is a place. Only the right answer actually answers "who," so it stands out.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone.

findings.problem: This card asks the baker to pick the exact wording of the psalm's opening line. Card 1 never showed that wording. It only said the writer was talking to his own soul. This tests wording the baker has not seen, not movement or meaning. A better question would ask what it means that the psalm ends the way it began, or what the writer calls his soul to do.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates both stops by a wide margin. Stop 1 has 8 multiple choice, 1 true or false and 1 fill in the blank. Stop 2 has 8 multiple choice, 1 true or false and 2 fill in the blank.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.
